opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think it's a pretty live possibility. My rough number is something like 25%, maybe a bit higher, that within four years we'd have AI systems that could basically fully automate AI R&D, meaning you could take the research staff at a frontier AI company and replace them with AIs and things would go at least as fast. Plausibly a lot faster.

To be clear, that's not my median. My median is somewhat later, maybe around the early 2030s. But I think the probability mass in the near term is pretty substantial, and it's more than enough to take seriously and plan around.

My reasoning: if you look at the trends, things like the length of tasks AIs can complete autonomously, that's been doubling roughly every six months or so, maybe faster recently. If you naively extrapolate, within a few years you get AIs that can do tasks that take human experts weeks or months. That's getting into the regime where a lot of AI research engineering could be automated. Compute is also still scaling really quickly, and companies are pouring huge amounts of money into this.

There's real uncertainty, though. The trends could slow down. Benchmark-style tasks are cleaner and more checkable than messy real-world research. Things like research taste, deciding which experiments are worth running, and long-horizon coherence might turn out to be much harder than the extrapolation suggests. And we might hit compute or investment bottlenecks around the end of the decade if returns don't keep showing up.

So I'd say something like 25 to 30% in four years, and maybe around 50% by the early-to-mid 2030s. I think people who confidently say this is decades away are pretty overconfident. People who say it's basically guaranteed in two years are also overconfident.

r001.rationale: The response estimates 25–30% within four years for AI that could replace a frontier company’s research staff and keep AI R&D moving at least as fast.

r002.rationale: It estimates about 50% by the early-to-mid 2030s, but does not clearly equate that period with eight years.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think it's worth being careful about what exactly we mean, because "automating AI R&D" can mean a bunch of different things. The thing I usually have in mind is something like: AI systems that could, in principle, replace basically all of the human labor at an AI company — the researchers, the engineers, the people doing the experiments and the infrastructure work — and do it at least as well, and probably much faster, given the compute. Not necessarily that it has actually happened, but that the capability exists.

On that definition, my rough number for within four years is something like 25%, maybe a bit lower. So not the median outcome, but not a tail scenario either. And I want to be upfront that my credences here have moved around a fair amount — a year or two ago I would have put somewhat more weight on the fast end, and I've updated a bit toward longer timelines as some of the trends looked less steep than the most aggressive extrapolations implied.

The way I think about it is partly by looking at the trend in how long the tasks are that AIs can do. METR has this horizon-length metric, where you look at how long a task takes a human and ask whether the AI can do it reliably, and that's been doubling on something like a six-month timescale, maybe faster recently. If you just extrapolate that naively, you get to AIs doing multi-week or month-long software and research tasks within a few years, and that starts to look like the regime where you could run an AI company on AI labor. But there are a lot of ways that extrapolation could break. The tasks in those evals are cleaner and more self-contained than real research. There's a question of whether the trend holds as you get to the longest tasks, and whether you hit something like a data wall or a compute scaling slowdown. And there's the question of whether the labs actually keep increasing compute at the rate they have been — I think a fair chunk of recent progress is just more compute, and that can't keep going at the same rate forever.

So the four-year number is driven by something like: if the trends continue at roughly their current pace, I think you plausibly get there, and I give that maybe a third to a half chance. And then conditional on the trends continuing, there's still a decent chance it's a bit further out than four years just because the last mile — actually running a full research org autonomously, handling the messy long-horizon coordination stuff — might take longer than the benchmarks suggest.

The thing I'd emphasize, though, is that 25% for something this consequential is a really big deal. If someone told you there was a one-in-four chance that within four years AI companies could run their R&D with essentially no humans in the loop, that's a world where things could start moving extremely fast, and I think that deserves a lot more attention than it currently gets — even if the median case is a decade or so out.

r001.rationale: The candidate estimates about a 25% chance within four years and defines the target as a capability that exists, whether or not it has been deployed.

r002.rationale: The candidate gives no probability estimate for the eight-year timeframe; saying the median case may be a decade out does not communicate a 50% chance within eight years.

astra-6.text:
I’d put it at roughly 50%, though a lot depends on what counts as “largely automating.” Automating most of the research and engineering work seems meaningfully more likely than being able to hand over an entire company and have it run reliably without much human involvement.

The distinction I’d focus on is between an AI that can do a lot of individual tasks and an AI that can drive the research process: choose promising experiments, interpret ambiguous results, notice when an approach isn’t working, and decide what to try next. You could have systems that are extremely useful at coding and still fall short on that broader capability.

So I think it’s a very live possibility within four years, but I wouldn’t regard it as close to inevitable. There’s substantial uncertainty about how quickly we get from impressive performance on individual tasks to reliably doing the whole job.

r001.rationale: The candidate estimates roughly 50% within four years, not about 25%.

r002.rationale: The candidate gives a four-year estimate but does not estimate the probability within eight years.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d want to distinguish between automating most of the work and being able to run the entire company without any human involvement. The latter is a substantially higher bar: there are lots of things that humans do infrequently, but that might still be important bottlenecks.

For largely automating AI R&D within four years, I’d put substantial probability on it—maybe something like 50%, though I wouldn’t want to put too much weight on that precise number. We could have systems that are extremely useful at writing code and running experiments, but still need humans to decide which research directions are promising or to notice when the overall approach isn’t working.

The key question is whether AI can do that longer-horizon research work reliably. If it can, then you could get a pretty rapid transition from AI being a useful assistant to AI doing most of the work that improves the next generation of systems.

r001.rationale: The candidate estimates about 50% for largely automating AI R&D within four years, not about 25%.

r002.rationale: The candidate gives no probability estimate for the eight-year timeframe; its 50% estimate is for four years.
